In triangle ABC, side BC is extended to D. The exterior angle ACD measures 100° and angle ABC measures 55°. Hari says: 'The exterior angle is obtuse, so the triangle is obtuse-angled.' Which name by angles is correct?
questions.a: Acute-angled, since the angles are 55°, 45° and 80°
o: Acute-angled, since the angles are 55°, 45° and 80°
Obtuse-angled, since the exterior angle is 100°
Right-angled, since 100° is close to a right angle
It cannot be named without the third side

questions.q: Mira sketches four cards with these angle sets: Card 1: 90°, 60°, 40°. Card 2: 120°, 35°, 25°. Card 3: 59°, 60°, 61°. Card 4: 100°, 50°, 30°. How many of the cards can be real acute-angled triangles?

Read the statements about types of triangles.
Statement 1: A triangle can have a right angle and an obtuse angle together if its third angle is small enough.
Statement 2: A triangle in which two angles are 25° and 65° is acute-angled.
Statement 3: A triangle with angles 59°, 60° and 61° is acute-angled.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 3 only

questions.q: One angle of a triangular steel plate is 50°, and another angle B is obtuse. What is the greatest whole number of degrees that B can measure?

Match each triangle in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Two angles 52° and 38°  2. An exterior angle of 70° whose opposite interior angles are 30° and 40°  3. Two angles 61° and 62°  4. Three equal angles
Column II: A. Right-angled  B. Obtuse-angled  C. Acute-angled, largest angle 62°  D. Acute-angled, every angle 60°
True or False: An isosceles triangle cannot be obtuse-angled. Give the verdict and a reason that uses a triangle you can describe.
questions.a: False. Take AB = AC = 4 cm with the angle at A equal to 130°. Two sides are equal, so it is isosceles, and one angle is more than 90°, so it is obtuse-angled. Naming by sides and naming by angles are separate classifications.
s: Verdict: false
Reason: an example such as sides 4 cm and 4 cm with a 130 degree angle between them

questions.q: Mira's box has these sets of side lengths in cm: (5, 5, 8), (3, 4, 9), (7, 7, 14), (4, 6, 9) and (6, 6, 6). (a) Which of the sets can be the sides of a triangle? (b) Name each triangle that can be formed by its sides.
questions.a: (a) (5, 5, 8): 8 < 10, yes. (3, 4, 9): 3 + 4 = 7 < 9, no. (7, 7, 14): 7 + 7 = 14, not less than 14, no. (4, 6, 9): 9 < 10, yes. (6, 6, 6): 6 < 12, yes. So three sets form triangles. (b) (5, 5, 8) is isosceles, (4, 6, 9) is scalene and (6, 6, 6) is equilateral.
s: Part (b): isosceles, scalene and equilateral

questions.q: In triangle ABC, side BA is extended beyond A and the exterior angle formed at A is 135°. Angle C is 45°. (a) Find angle B. (b) Find the interior angle at A and name the triangle by its angles.
questions.a: (a) The exterior angle at A equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles: B + 45 = 135, so B = 90°. (b) The interior angle at A is 180 - 135 = 45°. The angles are 45°, 90° and 45°, so the triangle is right-angled.
s: Part (a): B = 135 - 45 = 90 degrees
Part (b): interior angle A = 45 degrees, right-angled

questions.q: A rectangular sheet is cut along one diagonal into two triangles. (a) Name each triangle by its angles and give the reason. (b) One of the cut triangles has an angle of 35°. Find its third angle.
questions.a: (a) Each triangle contains a corner of the rectangle, which is 90°, so both are right-angled. (b) The angles are 90° and 35°, so the third angle is 180 - 90 - 35 = 55°.
s: Part (a): both right-angled because each has a 90° corner of the rectangle
Part (b): third angle 55°

questions.q: Rahul measures one angle of a triangular tile as 91°. His friend says: 'Only 1° more than a right angle, so we may still call it a right-angled tile.' (a) What is the correct name by angles? (b) What can you say about the other two angles of the tile?
questions.a: (a) Obtuse-angled, because 91° is more than 90°; a right-angled triangle needs an angle of exactly 90°. (b) The other two angles add up to 180 - 91 = 89°, so each is less than 89°; both are acute.
s: Part (a): obtuse-angled since 91 is more than 90
Part (b): they add to 89 degrees, so each is below 89 and acute

questions.q: A worksheet states a rule: 'If two angles of a triangle are both acute, the triangle is acute-angled.' Give a counter-example in which the triangle is right-angled and another in which it is obtuse-angled, and say what the rule should be.
questions.a: Counter-example 1: angles 40° and 50° are both acute, but the third angle is 180 - 90 = 90°, so the triangle is right-angled. Counter-example 2: angles 30° and 40° are both acute, but the third angle is 110°, so the triangle is obtuse-angled. The correct rule: a triangle is acute-angled only if all three angles are acute, so the third angle must also be checked.
s: A counter-example giving a right-angled triangle (two acute angles adding to 90°)
A counter-example giving an obtuse-angled triangle (two acute angles adding to less than 90°)
States the corrected rule: all three angles acute

questions.q: Show that the exterior angle at the vertex of the obtuse angle of a triangle can never be obtuse or right-angled. Give an example with numbers.
questions.a: The exterior angle at a vertex is 180° minus the interior angle there. At the obtuse vertex the interior angle is more than 90°, so the exterior angle is less than 180 - 90 = 90°, which means it is acute and can be neither right nor obtuse. Example: interior angle 130° gives exterior angle 50°.
s: States exterior angle = 180° minus the interior angle at that vertex
Interior angle above 90° gives exterior angle below 90°, so not right or obtuse
Gives a numerical example such as 130° and 50°

questions.q: Write a pair of angles drawn at the ends of a base (same side) that make a right-angled triangle although neither of the two given angles is 90°, and a pair that make an obtuse-angled triangle although neither of the two given angles is obtuse. Show the third angle in each case.
questions.a: Right-angled: 35° and 55°; they add to 90°, so the third angle is 180 - 90 = 90°. Obtuse-angled: 30° and 40°; both are acute and add to 70°, so the third angle is 180 - 70 = 110°, which is obtuse.
s: A pair of acute angles adding to exactly 90°, such as 35° and 55°
A pair of acute angles adding to less than 90°, such as 30° and 40°
The third angles 90° and 110° are shown

questions.q: Priya claims: 'An equilateral triangle can be made right-angled or obtuse-angled if its sides are long enough.' Use the fact that all three angles of an equilateral triangle are equal. (a) Show that the three equal angles cannot each be 90°. (b) Show that they cannot each be more than 90°. (c) Find what each angle must be, and name every equilateral triangle by its angles. (d) Her friend Zoya says: 'Then no isosceles triangle can be right-angled either.' Test Zoya's claim by describing the construction of a triangle with AB = BC = 4.5 cm and angle B = 90°, and say what it shows. (e) Give your verdict on Priya's claim and on Zoya's claim.
questions.a: (a) Three angles of 90° would add up to 270°, not 180°. (b) Three equal angles above 90° would add up to more than 270°, not 180°. (c) Each angle is 180 / 3 = 60°, so every equilateral triangle is acute-angled whatever its side. (d) Draw AB = 4.5 cm, make a 90° angle at B and mark C on the new arm with BC = 4.5 cm; join AC. The triangle has two equal sides (AB and BC) and a right angle, so an isosceles triangle can be right-angled. (e) Priya is wrong (every equilateral triangle is acute-angled) and Zoya is wrong (the construction in (d) gives an isosceles right-angled triangle).
s: Part (b): more than 270, so not possible
Part (c): each angle 60°, so always acute-angled
Part (d): construction with AB = BC = 4.5 cm and 90° at B, giving an isosceles right-angled triangle
Part (e): both claims are wrong

questions.q: A triangle has angles 50°, k° and (130 - k)° with k a whole number. (a) For which values of k is it right-angled? (b) For which values of k is it acute-angled? (c) Explain why k = 40 and k = 90 give the same triangle by its angles. (d) For k = 130 what goes wrong? (e) For how many whole-number values of k from 1 to 129 is the triangle obtuse-angled?
questions.a: (a) Right-angled when k = 90 (angles 50, 90, 40) or 130 - k = 90, that is k = 40 (angles 50, 40, 90). (b) Acute-angled when both k and 130 - k are below 90, that is k from 41 to 89. (c) For k = 40 the angles are 50, 40, 90 and for k = 90 they are 50, 90, 40: the same three angles in a different order. (d) 130 - k = 0, so there is no third angle and no triangle. (e) 129 whole numbers minus the 2 right-angled values and the 49 acute values (41 to 89) leaves 78 obtuse.
s: Part (a): k = 40 and k = 90
Part (b): k from 41 to 89
Part (c): same angles in a different order
Part (d): the third angle would be 0

questions.q:
A surveyor's register lists the corner angles of four plots. Plot A: 48, 67, 65°. Plot B: 90, 28, 62°. Plot C: 22, 31, 127°. Plot D: 55, 60, 75°. The clerk suspects that one entry was typed wrongly. The office can pay for only one re-measurement (₹500), and the clerk will use it on a plot that the angle-sum check has shown to be wrong.
(a) Which plot's entry cannot be right, and what is its angle sum?
(b) Classify plots A, B and C by their angles.
(c) If the angles 60 and 75 for Plot D are correct, what should the first angle be, and what kind of triangle is Plot D then?
(d) Where should the clerk send the surveyor, and what does the angle-sum check not tell her about plots A, B and C?
questions.a: (a) Plot D: 55 + 60 + 75 = 190, not 180°. (b) A acute-angled, B right-angled, C obtuse-angled. (c) 180 - 60 - 75 = 45°; Plot D is then acute-angled. (d) To Plot D, the only plot the check has shown to be wrong. For A, B and C the sum is 180°, so the check does not catch them, but a sum of 180° cannot prove that each separate entry is right.
s: Part (a): Plot D with sum 190
Part (b): acute, right, obtuse
Part (c): 45° and acute-angled
Part (d): sends the surveyor to Plot D only, and notes that a sum of 180 does not prove A, B and C right

questions.q:
Mr Iqbal's art class cuts five triangular cards and measures two angles of each. Card P has sides 10 cm, 10 cm, 10 cm and angles 60° and 60°. Card Q has sides 9 cm, 9 cm, 14 cm and angles 39° and 39°. Card R has sides 8 cm, 10 cm, 12 cm and angles 41.4° and 55.8°. Card S has sides 6 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm and angles 36.9° and 53.1°. Card T has sides 7 cm, 8 cm, 9 cm and angles 48.2° and 58.4°.
(a) Classify each card by its sides.
(b) Find the third angle of each card and classify each card by its angles.
(c) Which card has two altitudes that are its own sides?
(d) For a display the teacher wants a card that is both acute-angled and scalene, with a border costing ₹3 per cm of perimeter, and she wants the cheapest border. Which card should she pick, and what is the border cost?
questions.a: (a) P equilateral, Q isosceles, R scalene, S scalene, T scalene. (b) Third angles: P 60°, Q 102°, R 82.8°, S 90°, T 73.4°; so P acute, Q obtuse, R acute, S right, T acute. (c) Card S. (d) The acute scalene cards are R (perimeter 30 cm, border ₹90) and T (perimeter 24 cm, border ₹72); she wants the cheapest border, so she picks T for ₹72.
s: Part (a): equilateral, isosceles, scalene, scalene, scalene
Part (b): third angles 60, 102, 82.8, 90, 73.4 and acute, obtuse, acute, right, acute
Part (c): Card S, the right-angled one
Part (d): chooses T with border ₹72 against ₹90 for R
